nameStory: The name 'jimsonweed' comes from a dark chapter in American history - the 1676 incident in Jamestown, Virginia, where British soldiers accidentally ate this plant and spent days in a delirious state. Originally called 'Jamestown weed,' it eventually became corrupted to 'jimsonweed.' The alternative name 'devil's trumpet' refers to its beautiful but sinister trumpet-shaped flowers that seem to call out with danger.
description: Jimsonweed is a robust, bushy annual plant that can grow 3-5 feet tall and wide, with an almost tropical appearance despite being found throughout New England. It produces large, dramatic white trumpet-shaped flowers that bloom upward and spiny, egg-shaped seed pods that look like medieval weapons. The entire plant has a coarse, weedy appearance with large, irregularly-toothed leaves that give off an unpleasant smell when crushed. This is an extremely poisonous plant that should never be touched or handled without gloves.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large white trumpet-shaped flowers, 3-4 inches long, that point upward like megaphones. They have five pointed petals fused into a tube and emit a sweet, heavy fragrance that's strongest at night.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive spiny green seed pods about the size of a walnut, covered in sharp thorns that feel like tiny daggers. When ripe, they split open into four sections revealing dozens of flat, kidney-shaped black seeds.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, coarse leaves up to 8 inches long with irregular, sharp teeth along the edges. They feel rough and slightly fuzzy, and smell rank and unpleasant when crushed - like a mix of peanut butter and something rotten.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Bushy, sprawling annual that branches widely from the base, creating a robust plant that looks almost shrub-like. The thick, green stems fork repeatedly and have a succulent feel when squeezed.

habitat: Look for jimsonweed in disturbed soils like roadsides, vacant lots, farm edges, and waste areas throughout New England. It thrives in rich, well-drained soil and full sun, often appearing in places where the ground has been recently disturbed. You'll frequently find it growing alongside other weedy species like lamb's quarters and pigweed in agricultural areas and urban edges.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge in late spring as the soil warms, starting as small rosettes with their characteristic toothed leaves. Early plants are less recognizable without their signature flowers.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with the spectacular white trumpet flowers opening mainly in evening and at night. The distinctive spiny seed pods begin forming as flowers fade throughout the summer.
seasonality.fall: Mature spiny seed pods split open to reveal black seeds, while the plant begins to decline with first frosts. The dried seed pods persist and are often the most noticeable feature in late fall.
seasonality.winter: Plants are killed by hard frost, leaving behind dried stems and scattered spiny seed pod remnants that may persist into early winter.

funFact: Jimsonweed flowers are night-shift workers - they open in the evening and close by mid-morning, releasing their strongest perfume in the dark to attract night-flying sphinx moths as pollinators. The flowers can actually be heard opening with a soft 'pop' on quiet summer evenings!
confusionNotes: The large white trumpet flowers might remind you of morning glories, but jimsonweed flowers point upward like horns while morning glories face outward or slightly downward. Remember: 'Devil's trumpets point to hell above, morning glories greet the sun with love.' The spiny seed pods are a dead giveaway - no morning glory ever produced anything so wickedly armed.
contextualKnowledge: This plant is a member of the notorious nightshade family, which includes tomatoes and potatoes as well as deadly nightshade. Despite its beauty, jimsonweed contains powerful toxins called tropane alkaloids that make it extremely dangerous - even touching it can cause skin irritation, and ingesting any part can be fatal. Always wear gloves when removing it from gardens, and never let children or pets near it.
compareHints: Jimsonweed is the most common Datura species in New England, distinguished from its relatives by its upward-facing white flowers and especially spiny seed pods. Sacred datura has much larger flowers and grows mainly in southwestern deserts, while other devil's trumpets typically have purple or yellow flowers. If you see white trumpet flowers pointing skyward with viciously spiny pods in New England, it's almost certainly jimsonweed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sacred datura differs from its relative jimsonweed (the only other Datura commonly found in New England) by having much larger flowers, gray-green fuzzy leaves instead of bright green smooth ones, and a perennial growth habit rather than being an annual.
Metel devil's trumpet has larger, more ornamental upward-facing flowers compared to its weedy cousin jimsonweed, which has smaller white or purple flowers and more deeply toothed leaves.
Unlike its cousin jimsonweed which has smooth leaves and upright white flowers, downy thorn-apple has that distinctive fuzzy texture and flowers that nod slightly downward.
